clue.text: Advance for half a month — barrier to overcome

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only its opening portion, the first two of a four-letter month name

blocks.note: a sub is an advance payment on wages
the first half of June or July
a gate is a barrier across an opening

explanation.surface: Someone has a fortnight to get past an obstacle, perhaps a hurdle at work.
explanation.walkthrough: A sub is British slang for an advance on your pay. Either June or July works for the month.
explanation.definitionFit: To subjugate a people is to conquer and bring them under control, a stronger synonym of overcome.

blocks.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
a common man's name, short for Edward

explanation.definitionFit: Sated means satisfied to the point of having eaten enough, so a sated diner is full.

clue.text: Steward may be hit without trouble

blocks.note: a biff is an informal word for a punch

explanation.surface: A household steward risks a beating if he can't avoid trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like it means lacking, but here it means outside: the word for a punch wraps around the trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A bailiff was historically a steward or agent managing an estate on a landowner's behalf.

clue.text: Soldiers follow a uniform — it glows

blocks.note: taken as written
Uniform is U in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Royal Artillery, abbreviated RA

explanation.definitionFit: An aura is a luminous haze or radiance surrounding a person or object, something that gives off a glow.

blocks.note: F is a musical key
oil paintings are called oils

explanation.definitionFit: To foil a plan is to thwart it, and to check an advance means the same: halt or block it.

clue.text: Races round a pole, initially producing something highly explosive

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds only TNT; 'initially producing' says the answer is the full name whose initials those letters are.
explanation.definitionFit: Trinitrotoluene, known as TNT, is a powerful chemical explosive used in demolition and munitions.

explanation.definitionFit: A dais is a raised platform in a hall, a stand on which speakers or dignitaries sit.

explanation.surface: An absurd pile-up of soldiers, ending with toy soldiers in brackets.
explanation.walkthrough: The repetition is the joke: three of the four soldier words supply pieces, and only the last is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A regiment is a permanent army unit made up of many troops, a body of soldiers.

clue.text: Cook a carrot — it's for a privileged man

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Preparing a humble vegetable for a lord's dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: An aristocrat is a member of the nobility, a class enjoying inherited rank and privilege.

clue.text: Viewing gal dancing for sufficient pay

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and settle in a different arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man pays to watch a girl dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at a dancer's wages, which is close to the answer's own meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A living wage is a level of pay high enough to cover a worker's basic cost of living.

clue.text: Queen points to iron — King returns it repeatedly

clue.text: Force one to wear coat for a spell

blocks.note: a mac is a raincoat, short for mackintosh
g is the symbol for gravitational force
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'For a spell' reads as 'for a while'; spell is the enchantment. A mac is a British raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Magic is the power of enchantment, and a spell is a charm worked by it, so the two stand for each other.

clue.text: Blows top of straw in bottle

in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: bottle is British slang for courage, as is guts
the opening letter of straw

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' meaning nerve is British slang. The single letter goes inside the four-letter word after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusts are sudden strong rushes of wind, each one a blow.

blocks.note: a sponge is a light cake

explanation.surface: A cake recipe uncovers some creature living off the cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponger lives off others' generosity without contributing, a human parasite.

clue.text: I see you in conversation at a section of the hospital

indicators.note: in conversation means as spoken, so the words are to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: spoken, these words sound like three letters forming a well-known hospital abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone tells a friend they spotted them, mid-chat, in a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: Said out loud, 'I see you' is the three letters ICU, the standard short form of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An intensive care unit is the hospital ward where critically ill patients receive constant monitoring.

blocks.note: Benjamin Disraeli, Victorian British prime minister

explanation.walkthrough: 'National' reads as an adjective but is a noun, a citizen of a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: An Israeli is a citizen of Israel, a national of that country.

blocks.note: to net a fish is to catch it
the Foreign Office, the British diplomatic service

explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch up with' is a phrasal verb in the surface; here 'up' turns both pieces around together.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means frequently or many times, the sense of regularly here.

blocks.note: a peek is a quick look

taken as written
